Brønsted Acid-Catalyzed Aza-Ferrier Reaction of N,O‑Allenyl Acetals:
Synthesis of β‑Amino-α-methylene Aldehydes
Eiji Tayama * and Yuki Ishikawa
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2020, 85, 9405 −9414 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: AT f 2NH-catalyzed aza-Ferrier reaction of N,O-
allenyl acetals was reported. This protocol provided various types
of β-amino-α-methylene aldehydes as the products. The N,O-
allenyl acetal substrates were easily prepared by base-induced
isomerization of N,O-propargyl acetals with Triton B. The N,O-
propargyl acetals were prepared from the corresponding aldehydes
or lactams. Further synthetic applications of the products were also described.
T
he acid-catalyzed aza-Ferrier reaction of N,O-alkenyl
acetals is an atom-economical reaction that proceeds via
acid-catalyzed cleavage of the C −O bond to generate the
corresponding iminium ion as an electrophile and the enolate
(Lewis acid) or the enol (Brønsted acid) as a nucleophile
(Scheme 1 a).
1 Sequential C −C bond formation provides the
corresponding β-amino aldehydes, which act as valuable
building blocks for the synthe sis of biologically active
compounds such as β-amino acids and alkaloids. Initial studies
on this reaction were carried out by Frauenrath et al. 2 Their
group reported the Lewis acid-catalyzed reaction of N,O-
alkenyl acetals to a ﬀord α-substituted-β-amino aldehydes. Our
group applied this protocol to the reaction of N,O-1,3-dienyl
acetals as substrates and obtained β-amino-β′,γ′-unsaturated
aldehydes.3 The enantio- and diastereoselective reaction was
achieved by Terada ’s group using a chiral Brønsted acid
catalyst.4 However, from a synthetic point of view, this reaction
has a disadvantage in the preparation of N,O-alkenyl moieties
because e ﬃcient preparative methods of these moieties have
been limited. The preparations were conducted using N,O-
allylic acetals as a precursor by (i) base-induced isomerization,
(ii) transition-metal-catalyzed isomerization, or (iii) base-
promoted elimination. These methods limit the substrate and
product scopes; therefore, further studies and development of
the aza-Ferrier reaction have not been advanced.
To progress the study on the aza-Ferrier reaction, we
focused on two previous works: (i) Lewis acid-catalyzed
Ferrier reaction of O,O-allenyl acetals into β-alkoxy- α-
methylene aldehydes reported by Ricci et al. ( Scheme 1 b)
5
and (ii) e ﬃcient and simple isomerization of O,O-propargyl
acetals into O,O-allenyl acetals with benzyltrimethylammo-
nium hydroxide (Triton B) reported by Ishikawa et al.
(Scheme 1 c).
6 These works gave us the idea of an aza version
of these transformations from N,O-propargyl acetals 1 into β-
amino-α-methylene aldehydes 3 via N,O-allenyl acetals 2
(Scheme 1d).7 Although the structures of products 3 are in the
same category as those of the products obtained by the aza-

Morita−Baylis−Hillman (aza-MBH) reaction, 8 we believed
that our protocol would expand the product library. The main
product examples of aza-MBH reactions are limited to β-aryl
derivatives because the reaction requires the use of an imine as
the substrate. Preparable and chemically stable aromatic imines
are strongly preferred. Therefore, we started to investigate the
acid-catalyzed aza-Ferrier reaction of N,O-allynyl acetals 2 to
provide various types of β-amino-α-methylene aldehydes 3.
First, we tried to prepare N,O-allenyl acetal 2a by the
traditional base-induced isomerization of N,O-propargyl acetal
1a
9 with tBuOK.10 The exact reason is unclear currrently, and
the yield of desired 2a was low, with the recovery of 1a and
small amounts of decomposition materials. Thus, we
attempted to use Triton B for the isomerization according to
the literature,
6 as depicted in Scheme 1 c. This reagent was
found to be quite e ﬀective for isomerization of 1a (Scheme 2).
A commercially available MeOH solution of Triton B was
evaporated and dried under a vacuum. The residue and 1a in
DMSO were stirred at room temperature to give desired 2a in
an 84% yield. Other derivatives 2b−l were also prepared under
the same conditions.
With the substrates in hand, we investigated the aza-Ferrier
reactions of N,O-allenyl acetal 2a in CH2Cl2 at −78 °C for 1 h
in the presence of 10 mol % Lewis or Brønsted acid catalysts
(Table 1). First, we selected the standard Lewis acid BF
3·OEt2,
and the reaction gave desired β-amino-α-methylene aldehyde
3a in a 53% yield (entry 1). The use of Sc(OTf) 3 did not
improve the yield of 3a (entry 2). Cu(OTf) 2 did not show
catalytic activity under the conditions used (entry 3). The
reactions in the presence of standard Brønsted acids such as p-
TsOH·H
2O and PPTS resulted in failure (entries 4 and 5).
Decomposition or recovery of substrate 2a was observed.
However, when the reaction was carried out with the stronger
Brønsted acid Tf
2NH,11 the yield of 3a was dramatically
improved to 93% (entry 6). These conditions were found to be
applicable for an experiment on a scale greater than 1 mmol
(entry 7, 93% yield). With lower catalytic amounts (1 or 5 mol
%) of Tf
2NH, the yields of 3a were decreased (entries 8 and
9).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we prepared a series
of substrates 2b−l and carried out their reactions to de ﬁne the
scope and limitations of the present aza-Ferrier reaction of
N,O-allenyl acetals ( Scheme 3). The reactions of substrates 2b
and 2c bearing removable substituent R
1 on the nitrogen atom,
such as N-benzyl and N-allyl, proceeded to give 3b and 3c,
respectively, in good yields. Next, we investigated the reactions
of 2d−j bearing di ﬀerent types of substituent R
2 to obtain
various types of β-amino-α-methylene aldehydes 3d−j. The
reactions of substrate 2 with a simple substituent, such as 2d
(R2 = nBu) and 2e (R2 = Me), proceeded with excellent yields
(3d, 91%; 3e, 89%). Interestingly, the reaction of 2f (R2 =
CH2Ph) produced the corresponding product 3f in 75% yield,
although the intermediate iminium ion generated from 2f has
acidic and isomerizable benzylic protons. To compare with the
aza-MBH reaction, we investigated the reaction of aryl
derivative 2g (R
2 = Ph) to produce 3g, which is the standard
structure of the aza-MBH reaction product. The reaction rate
observed by TLC analysis was slow; thus, the yield of 3g was
low (69%). The reactions were not a ﬀected by a secondary
alkyl substituent, such as isopropyl 2h (R
2 = iPr) and
unsubstituted 2i (R2 = H) derivatives, and produced 3h
(89%) and 3i (81%), respectively. We considered the reaction
of the tert-butyl derivative (R 2 = tBu); however, the
preparation of the corresponding substrate 2 was unsuccessful.
A failure example was the reaction of (+)-citronellyl derivative
2j (R
2 = (+)-citronellyl). The desired 3j was obtained in only a
2% yield, with the formation of various side products observed

2NH, with the resulting carbocation causing side
reactions. Finally, we attempted the reactions of N-heterocyclic
derivatives 2k and 2l and obtained the corresponding β-amino-
α-methylene aldehydes 3k (94%) and 3j (93%). These
compounds may act as valuable building blocks for the
synthesis of alkaloid analogues.
With these results in hand, further synthetic transformations
of products 3 were demonstrated ( Scheme 4 ). Wittig
oleﬁnation of 3e with methylene ylide provided 2-substi-
tuted-1,3-butadiene 4 in a 78% yield, and Diels −Alder reaction
with 1,4-naphthoquinone gave the corresponding adduct 5 in
an 85% yield ( Scheme 4 a). Cyclic product 3l could be
transformed into 1,3-oxazine derivative 7 by 1,2-hydride
reduction into 6 in an 88% yield, followed by base-promoted
cyclization in a 74% yield ( Scheme 4 b). We attempted the
same transformation using acyclic 3a; however, the cyclization
resulted in failure. Finally, the Michael addition of diethyl
malonate into α-methylene aldehyde 3i aﬀorded α-substituted-
β-aminoaldehyde derivative 8 in a 79% yield ( Scheme 4 c).
In conclusion, the Tf
2NH-catalyzed aza-Ferrier reaction of
N,O-allenyl acetals 2 is reported. This protocol provides
various types of β-amino-α-methylene aldehydes 3 as the
products. Products 3 act as valuable building blocks, and
further synthetic applications were successfully demonstrated,
such as Wittig ole ﬁnation followed by the Diels −Alder
reaction, 1,2-reduction followed by cyclization, and Michael
addition. The substrates N,O-allenyl acetals 2 were easily
prepared by base-induced isomerization of N,O-propargyl
acetals 1 with Triton B. Our protocol would expand the
product library of β-amino-α-methylene aldehydes.
